content.thinking:
I should draft the postmortem noting the incident is still unresolved so duration and impact figures are lower bounds, that the rollback attempt failed since there was no prior revision, and that it's now escalated to humans. I want the executive summary to avoid naming specific components, and I need to flag my assumptions clearly: I'm treating the payment provider's 503s as originating upstream without verifying provider status, assuming no deploy/config/flag changes occurred since there's no record of any, and treating all duration/impact numbers as lower bounds only.

For the actual figures, I shouldn't present the given percentages as if I computed them myself, nor should I invent new numbers — better to describe things qualitatively, like saying nearly all account page requests failed, which reflects what the logs show without claiming a calculation I didn't do.

assumptions: The outage duration and every impact figure are lower bounds: the service had not recovered by the last minute of metrics available, so the true end time and total customer impact are unknown.

The 503s are assumed to originate at the payment provider itself. The provider's own status was never checked directly; the conclusion rests on the shop's client-side error logs plus the absence of any recorded change on our side.
The absence of deploy, configuration and flag changes is taken from the change and flag histories returning no records. If a change was made outside those tracked systems, it would not appear.
No traffic, memory or dependency evidence other than the service's own metrics and logs was examined; the conclusion that the shop itself was healthy rests on those signals alone.
Argus held the incident for about half a minute before escalating; that is a measure of response time and says nothing about how long the service was broken.

No successful mitigation was applied. The only action attempted (configuration rollback) failed outright, so the service's return to health, whenever it occurred, is not attributable to anything Argus did.
input.executive_summary:
Starting at 23:43 UTC on 22 September 2026, the account page of the online shop stopped working for essentially everyone who tried to load it. The page depends on an outside card-payment company to show a shopper's saved card details; that company's service began rejecting every request, and because the page cannot render without it, shoppers saw errors instead of their account instead of a partially working page. Pages also became very slow before failing, as the shop waited on and retried the unresponsive provider.

Monitoring raised the alert about five minutes after the failure began, and the automated responder picked it up within a second and diagnosed it within half a minute. The responder confirmed from the service's own records that nothing had been changed or released on the shop recently, which ruled out our own software as the trigger. It attempted one automated remedy — reverting the shop to its previous configuration — which failed because there was no earlier configuration to revert to, and in any case would not have helped, since the fault is outside our systems. The incident was then escalated to on-call engineers.

The failure was still ongoing at the last point for which we have data, so the outage lasted at least as long as the roughly five-minute window we can see, and all impact figures quoted in the alert are floors rather than totals. Nothing an automated tool can do resolves this class of failure: recovery depends on the payment provider, or on a person disabling or degrading the card section of the account page. Follow-up work should focus on making the account page render without card details when the provider is unavailable, and on alerting on payment-provider health directly rather than waiting for the customer-facing error rate to cross a threshold.
input.root_cause: At 23:43 UTC the external payment provider (api.io-pay.example) began returning HTTP 503 to every /v1/shoppers/*/card request, and io-shop's account page has no fallback or circuit-breaker for that call, so the upstream failure propagated straight through to shoppers as errors (with latency rising to the upstream timeout/retry ceiling). No deploy, configuration or feature-flag change was recorded on io-shop in the lookback window, and traffic and memory were flat, so nothing internal to the service was implicated.
